A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RealCam-I2V and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Content can be matched despite substantial reorganization and additional experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original RealEstate10K comparisons, component ablations, VBench-I2V evaluations, and generated-video examples.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds noise-threshold experiments and RealCam-Vid/CogVideoX results in its appendices.

M1.justification: The depth alignment, interactive camera trajectories, masked scene guidance, and interpolation/continuation procedures remain. v2 expresses guidance in noisy-latent form and explicitly documents per-step noise resampling; this does not establish a changed underlying implementation. CogVideoX is presented as another application of the framework.

E1.justification: v2 adds training on RealCam-Vid, covering dynamic scenes with metric-scale camera annotations and large movements approaching 360 degrees (Section 4.1 and Appendix E/Table 5). This substantially extends the predominantly static RealEstate10K training coverage. RealEstate10K, VBench-I2V, and the existing application tasks remain.

E2.justification: The main DynamiCrafter, MotionCtrl, CameraCtrl, and CamI2V comparator set remains. v2 adds a CogVideoX 1.5 control in Table 5 and removes the official DynamiCrafter row from the VBench comparison, retaining the reproduced version (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 3).

E3.justification: The original splits, 1,000-sample evaluation, frame sampling, metrics, and stated training-step budget remain. Added experiments introduce CogVideoX 1.5 and Metric3D v2 configurations, reported MonST3R checks, and a noise-shaping threshold sweep. These extend the evaluation settings rather than replace the main protocol.

E4.justification: Appendix D/Table 4 adds quantitative analysis of the camera-control versus dynamics tradeoff across noise thresholds, beyond v1's qualitative illustration. Appendix E adds a portability experiment jointly changing data, backbone, and depth predictor, plus qualitative SfM robustness reports. Existing component ablations and the boundary-filter example remain; the latter moves to the appendix.

E5.justification: Both versions report five SfM trials per video and average successful trials before averaging across samples. Neither adds generation-seed reporting, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Main results are revised: Table 1 RealCam-I2V VideoGPT FVD changes from 55.229 to 53.718, and CamI2V RotErr from 0.4968 to 0.4120. MotionCtrl's main-table values are reconciled with its existing ablation values. The CamI2V alignment-only relative-error trends reverse, and Tables 4–5 add threshold and dynamic-data results. These are revised and additional reports, not an isolated cross-version performance comparison.

T1.justification: The geometric projection, scale alignment, diffusion objective, and camera-error definitions retain their mathematical substance. The noise-shaping expression is recast using the existing forward-noise relation. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive derivations appear.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: scale-consistent camera control, interactive trajectory design, scene-constrained guidance, improved generation quality, and interpolation/looping applications. Replacing 'absolute' with 'metric' largely changes terminology, while new experiments support retained contributions.

C2.justification: v1 identifies poorer performance on anime, paintings, and cartoon-like styles; v2 instead emphasizes cross-style and dynamic-scene generalization and attributes remaining limitations to data scarcity. Appendix E newly argues that consistently propagated depth errors prevent training–inference scale gaps and discusses broader predictor, SfM, and backbone applicability.

D1.justification: v2 adds noise-resampling, threshold-selection, and parallel preview-rendering/streaming details. Reported training time changes from about 25 to 50 hours, while the eight-H100 hardware specification disappears; batch size and training steps remain. The explicit promise to release annotations, code, and checkpoints is also removed, although the project-page pointer remains.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands coverage of recent video foundation models and datasets, including HunyuanVideo, GoKu, Open-Sora, and Panda-70M. v2 also acknowledges AC3D alongside 4DiM as using metric-depth estimation to address scale inconsistency, replacing v1's narrower positioning of 4DiM as a novel-view-synthesis exception.

P1.justification: The method is reorganized around the base model, metric alignment, and one-round inference. Related work and limitations are rewritten, terminology changes throughout, appendices are reordered and expanded, and the societal-impact section is removed. These are substantial structural and explanatory revisions.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the opening overview and pipeline, adds camera-ambiguity, workflow, and preview illustrations, and replaces application displays. Tables are reordered and reformatted, with two new appendix tables. The filtering illustration moves to the appendix, while the original qualitative noise-shaping comparison disappears.

improvement.justification: v2 improves evidential support through quantitative noise-threshold analysis and the dynamic-data/second-backbone experiment, while clarifying the workflow and acknowledging closer prior work. The net gain is limited by sparse details for the new experiment, removed hardware information, and reporting inconsistencies: dynamic-data training remains described as future work despite Table 5, and the no-noise camera-motion score differs between Tables 3 and 4.
